news.2026-10-19-chine-croissance-exports: China speeds up thanks to exports, but its people still spend little
China's economy grew 4.5% between July and September, better than expected. Sales abroad are driving growth, not household spending.
China reports 4.5% year-on-year growth for the third quarter, above forecasts. In the second quarter it was 4.3%, the slowest pace in more than three years [1][2].
Exports carried the quarter. According to AP's analysis, China is on track to beat last year's record trade surplus of $1.2 trillion [1].

Domestic demand remains weak, weighed down by a property crisis that has lasted for years. An economist quoted by AP even calls this growth figure "an increasingly poor indicator" of how healthy the economy is [1].
The number is good, but it hides an imbalance: China produces a lot and sells the surplus to the rest of the world, while its own people consume little [1].

Beijing has set a growth target of 4.5% to 5% for 2026, and the IMF has just cut its own forecast to 4.5%, right at the bottom of the target [1]. The more China exports, the more its partners, Europe first, worry about their factories being undercut.
When China sells more than it buys, its products flood into Europe at low prices: that is good for your wallet, but it puts pressure on European factories and fuels the debates on tariffs.

news.2026-10-19-guyana-croissance-petrol: Guyana: the small country growing by almost 24% a year thanks to its oil
The World Bank raises its 2026 growth forecast for Guyana to 23.7%, the fastest in the region, driven by offshore oil.
In its October update on Latin America and the Caribbean, the World Bank forecasts 23.7% growth for Guyana in 2026. In April it said 16.3% [1][2].
The country's economy had already grown by 33.8% in 2023 and 43.8% in 2024, and the Bank estimates 19.3% for 2025 [1].
The government is more cautious: its 2026 budget assumes 16.2% growth, with oil up 17.9%, or about 840,000 barrels a day against 715,000 in 2025 [3].
The engine is oil pumped off the coast: the World Bank says Guyana alone pulls up growth for the whole sub-region [1].

The gap between 23.7% (World Bank) and 16.2% (government) is a reminder that a forecast is not a result. And a country that depends this much on one resource stays exposed if the oil price or production falls [1][3].
When the barrel gets pricier, as it is now, some small oil-producing countries get rich very fast. But that income depends on a single resource: if the price or output falls, growth drops back.

news.2026-10-19-cacao-cote-divoire-ghana: Cocoa: Côte d'Ivoire cuts the price paid to farmers by 57%, Ghana raises it
After the price collapse, the world's two biggest cocoa producers make opposite choices. Ivorian farmers will get much less, Ghanaian farmers a little more.
Côte d'Ivoire confirmed on 2 September that farmers would receive 1,200 CFA francs per kilo for the 2026-2027 season, 57% less than the 2,800 francs at the start of the previous season [1].
Ghana does the opposite: it slightly raised its price, to 42,400 cedis a tonne, thanks to a new law guaranteeing producers at least 70% of the export value of their beans [1].
Both countries face the same shock: cocoa hit a record of $12,906 a tonne in December 2024, then fell below $3,000 in February 2026. Both also sell much of their crop in advance [1].
The usual explanation is financial: Côte d'Ivoire had sold part of its crop in advance at low prices, while Ghana had already cut its price in February [1].

The author of the analysis adds another reason: the balance of power between farmers, the state and buyers is not the same in the two countries [1]. For millions of families, it is the difference between an income that holds and one that collapses.
Cocoa is the raw material of chocolate. When world prices soar and then fall back, it is West African farmers who take the hit, long before the price of your bar changes.

news.2026-10-19-serbie-nis-raffinerie-sa: Serbia: the country's only refinery runs on a US waiver until 30 October
Serbian oil company NIS, owned by Russians, is under US sanctions. Washington lets it keep importing crude until it is sold to a Hungarian group.

Serbia has obtained a new sanctions waiver from the United States for NIS: the company can keep importing crude oil until 30 October, pending the sale of its Russian majority stake to Hungary's MOL [1].
NIS runs Serbia's only refinery, which covers about 80% of the country's needs [1].

Washington sanctioned NIS in October 2025 to hit Russian energy, and demanded that Gazprom Neft and Gazprom sell their stakes, 56% in total. MOL signed a provisional agreement in January and committed to keeping the Pančevo refinery open [1][2].
The oil arrives through the Janaf pipeline, which crosses Croatia: without US permission, this tap can be shut. And it is not yet known whether the waiver will be extended or the sale completed [1].
It is an example of how sanctions target one company... and hit a whole country that depends on it for fuel [1][2].

Sanctions don't only hit Russia: they spill over to third countries and their fuel prices. It is the same kind of chain that links decisions taken in Washington to the price of a full tank across Central Europe.

news.2026-10-19-malaisie-ue-libre-echang: Malaysia–Europe: the free trade deal is 80% done, but palm oil still blocks it
Kuala Lumpur aims to sign with the European Union by the end of June 2027. Talks have run since 2010, and the deal would not apply before 2029.

Malaysia's trade minister, Johari Abdul Ghani, announced on 13 October that his country wants to sign the agreement with the European Union by the end of June 2027. Nearly 80% of the negotiations are done [1].
Talks began in 2010, were blocked in 2012 after seven rounds over disagreements on palm oil, then resumed in 2025 after an announcement by Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and Ursula von der Leyen [1].

According to an MVO analysis, the agreement would probably not apply before the second half of 2029: legal review, translation and ratification will take at least 18 to 24 months. And the EU-Indonesia deal already gives Indonesian palm oil preferential access [2].
Palm oil is the heart of the issue: Europe sets environmental rules and Malaysia thinks they penalise its flagship product [1][2].
Every deal signed by a competitor disadvantages those without one. Malaysia is therefore in a hurry, or it will pay higher tariffs than Indonesia during the transition period [2].
Palm oil is in many everyday products (biscuits, spreads, cosmetics). A deal could make trading it easier, but it has to balance trade with forest protection, a subject Europeans watch closely.

news.2026-10-19-iran-plan-sept-jours-orm: Iran: the seven-day plan to reopen Hormuz stays on the table, Washington doubts it
Tehran offers to reopen the strait in exchange for an end to the US naval blockade and relief from oil sanctions. The Iranian minister says the offer still stands.
Iran has presented the United States, through intermediaries, a seven-day plan: halt the fighting, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart nuclear negotiations [3].

According to Minister Abbas Araghchi, the first steps would take four to five days, the strait would reopen on day six and talks on a final deal would begin on day seven. In exchange, Tehran asks for the lifting of the US naval blockade, a waiver on its oil sales and the release of about $12 billion in assets [2][3].

The US State Department says the strait is already open, and Mike Pompeo calls the offer "likely not a serious proposal". The Wall Street Journal reported that Donald Trump had rejected it. On 18 October, Abbas Araghchi repeated that the proposal remained on the table [1][2][3].

The two sides don't even describe the situation the same way: for Washington, Hormuz is open; for Tehran, you have to negotiate to reopen it [3]. As long as this disagreement lasts, tankers hesitate and the barrel stays expensive.
The plan links three sticking points: the strait, the nuclear programme and sanctions. A deal on one would force progress on the other two [2][3].
Hormuz is a key passage for Gulf oil. When it is uncertain, the price of the fuel you pay for in France can rise a few weeks later.

news.2026-10-19-ukraine-locomotives-ble-: Ukraine: short of locomotives, the country struggles to export its wheat and iron
Russian strikes on trains have almost emptied the locomotive reserve. Kyiv is looking for engines from European countries that use the same rail gauge.

According to the Financial Times, citing Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi, Ukraine has almost used up its locomotive reserve because of Russian strikes. Kyiv is talking with European countries that have the same rail gauge [1][2].
Russia has stepped up attacks on trains carrying wheat and iron ore, two major Ukrainian exports. Port operator TIS lost three locomotives near the port of Pivdennyi [1][2].

Since the start of the invasion, 533 Ukrzaliznytsia locomotives and 75 belonging to private companies have been damaged, according to ministry data cited by Radio Liberty. Slovakia is offering three and Lithuania three more [3][1].
A wheat field is not enough: you need trains to bring the grain to the ports. Even if Black Sea ports work, the last rail link can block everything [1].
Authorities believe the available machines can keep the network running normally for now, but the spare reserve is almost used up [1][2].
Ukraine is a major grain exporter. If its trains run short, its deliveries of wheat and corn can slow down, which weighs on world food prices.

Kenya rescues its airline: 11 of its 34 planes are grounded
Kenya's government grants $350 million to Kenya Airways and turns part of its debt into equity. The airline is still looking for a strategic investor.

Kenya's government has approved a $350 million shareholder loan for Kenya Airways, repayable over up to ten years and convertible into equity. The money is meant to pay urgent debts and put planes back in service [1][2].
It also approved converting about 122 billion shillings (nearly $940 million) of public loans into an equity-like instrument. This brings no fresh money, but it lightens the airline's debt [1][2].

Eleven of the airline's 34 planes are grounded, including two Boeing 787-8s, with a return to service targeted for early 2027. It is seeking at least $1.5 billion from a strategic investor, expected in the first quarter of 2027 [1][2].
A national airline is a symbol, but also an economic tool: it links the country to the world for tourism, and for exported flowers or coffee. Without planes, these flows slow down [1].
The measures are still subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals: the rescue is therefore not finished [1].
Struggling state airlines are a classic, from Africa to Europe. It shows why governments hesitate between backing them with public money and letting them find a private partner.
